depth: The monocular depth map represents the corner kitchen's 3D structure by distinguishing the near foreground—the maroon-hooded person, shown in bright white/light grey at about 0.4 to 1.0 m and within the camera wearer's arm's reach from frame 2 onward, plus the vertical partition wall entering from the left in frames 3 through 5, around 0.4 to 0.7 m away and likewise within arm's reach—from the mid-ground upper cabinets, range hood, and countertop microwave, rendered medium grey at approximately 1.2 to 2.0 m and within the other person's arm's reach. It also separates these from the dark background ceiling and adjacent room beyond the partition, which are more than 2.5 m away. Across all five frames, the person and left wall edge grow brighter and larger, indicating that the camera wearer pans left and advances from about 1.0 m to 0.5 m, while the person moves from the lower-left edge toward center-right and changes from facing away in frames 1–3, to a profile in frame 4, to facing the camera wearer in frame 5. The map clearly shows the uninterrupted planar recession of the intersecting cabinet walls, the corner microwave's projecting box-shaped volume, and the abrupt depth break between the foreground partition and the deeper room on its left—features that are more difficult to measure from RGB alone. Still, it unreliably gives the person's head distinctly darker, farther values than the hoodie shoulders, produces bleeding depth halos around the motion-blurred head in frame 3, and merges small counter objects such as bottles and the dish rack into the background.
segmentation: The instance-segmentation view separates individual foreground and countertop objects from an unlabeled black background. It identifies the person in the lower foreground, approximately 0.4 to 1.0 m from the camera wearer and cropped at the chest/shoulders by the bottom border, together with kitchen objects located roughly 0.5 to 1.0 m behind them. In frame 1, the person at bottom-left partly blocks a purple mask covering the white range hood above, about 1.2 m away. In frame 2, after the person moves rightward into full view at roughly 0.7 m while facing away from the camera wearer, the map outlines a cyan bottle about 1.2 m away, immediately right of the person's shoulder and within their arm's reach, a purple microwave around 1.5 m away in the corner, and a bowl resting on the microwave. Frame 4 includes a green 'sink' mask at bottom-right, approximately 1.2 m away, while the person turns their head right; by frame 5, the close person alone is segmented at about 0.5 m while looking back toward the camera wearer. These pixel-level regions readily distinguish overlapping outlines, including the slim bottle between the person's right shoulder and the microwave in frame 2, which visually merges with the busy countertop in RGB. However, performance is inconsistent between frames: every object is missed amid frame 3's motion blur; the overhead range hood is incorrectly labeled 'microwave' in frame 1 and 'tv' in frame 2; the corner microwave region is wrongly tagged as a 'sink' in frame 4; and the cabinets, partition wall, and countertop clutter are excluded.
pose: Across the five frames, the body-and-hand skeleton visualization is nearly completely empty, showing only scattered, incomplete yellow body keypoints in frames 2 and 4 and never displaying any magenta hand skeletons. The person is extremely near the camera wearer, about 0.4 to 1.0 m away, and the egocentric frame's lower border hides everything below their upper chest, so their arms and hands stay entirely outside the image despite the kitchen counter and bottle being only around 0.4 to 0.6 m in front of them and therefore within their arm's reach. Frame 2 shows part of a yellow neck-and-shoulder structure near the lower-left while the person faces away toward the range hood. In frame 4, a small tangle of yellow torso/head segments appears around the bottom-center as the person turns their head right. Frames 1, 3, and 5 yield no detections at all, even though in frame 5 the person looks straight at the camera wearer from approximately 0.5 m away. Although the limited frame-2 and frame-4 detections broadly support the person's horizontal movement from the left toward center-right in the lower foreground, the pose visualization contributes no spatial information beyond RGB and remains very unreliable with severe lower-body cropping, rear-facing poses, and motion blur.
